name: PT Citra Borneo Utama Tbk

frontmatter.title: Citra Borneo Utama: a downstream palm processor priced as a leveraged trader
frontmatter.summary: CBUT refines palm products bought mainly from its SSMS parent group. The 2026 profit jump is real but thin: nine-month operating profit was IDR485.8bn on IDR14,140.0bn of revenue while IDR5,240.0bn of short-term bank loans sits against a IDR3,300.0bn pledged deposit. Netting that matched pair at face, our DCF puts the equity at Rp614 a share, well below the Rp1,005 price. SELL.
thesis: The 2026 profit jump is real but thin: operating profit of IDR485.8bn on IDR14,140.0bn of revenue is the run-rate we model, not a margin to be haircut [S2].

The restricted balance is not a haircut to argue about: the IDR3,300.0bn deposit cash-collateralises IDR5,240.0bn of short-term bank loans, so the matched pair nets at face and the economic liability is smaller than the gross debt line [S2, F13, F14].
The DCF, at a 11.4% WACC, is worth Rp614 a share with the collateral netted at face; the enterprise is worth more than the debt it carries, but not enough to justify the price [S0].
The price implies CPO 1.1 times our FY2027E deck on the same basis, so the market is paying for a spread above the one the audited accounts show [S0].
Ownership concentration cuts against the minority: SSMS holds 70.2%, free float is 19.6%, and related-party purchases of IDR10,574.5bn sit against cost of sales of IDR11,988.5bn [S7, S8].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: the first full year at the widened refining spread, and the test of whether working capital unwinds
AGM and dividend decision for FY2026
Q4-2026 LK and the 2027 CPO price outlook from IPOC/GAPKI

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp618, -38.5%, a capital-only return with no dividend assumed.** The shares trade at Rp1,005, a third below the year high of Rp1,580 [S0]. The business is not an estate: it is a refiner and trader of palm products that buys its feedstock from the SSMS group and sells refined olein, stearin, PFAD and kernel products into export and domestic channels [S7, S0].

The variant view is about the spread and the leverage, not the palm price and not a haircut on restricted cash. The market is paying for a 2026 margin that is thin rather than exceptional, and it reads the pledged deposit as trapped value; we net it at face against the IDR5,240.0bn of short-term bank loans it cash-collateralises, because a matched loan and collateral pair is one exposure, and what remains is IDR6,075.6bn of gross debt against a business whose nine-month operating profit was IDR485.8bn [S2, F13, F14]. The nine-month accounts show a gross margin of 21.6% on IDR14,140.0bn of revenue but operating profit of only IDR485.8bn; our FY2026E net profit of IDR377.9bn is in line with the nine-month annualisation, not above it [S2, S0]. Working capital is the second problem: inventory rose to IDR2,030.0bn and interest-bearing debt now dwarfs equity [S2].

Why the discount exists is legible. The stock is 19.6% free float with IDR0.4bn of daily turnover, the majority holder is a listed planter, and the company is a low-margin intermediary whose profits move with a processing spread few analysts model [S0, S7]. Our DCF, the primary method at a 11.4% WACC, gives Rp614 a share; the probability-weighted value before the liquidity discount is Rp773, and the target after the house's 20.0% discount for the thin tape is Rp618 [S0]. Every leg of the valuation sits below the price, so the call does not rest on which method the reader prefers.

What moves the value: a refining spread holding above the audited FY2025 level at a stable palm price; working capital unwinding without a refinancing; and the collateral being released on repayment rather than re-pledged into a renewed facility - a branch we disclose but do not quantify, and one the bear case does not carry: the bear keeps the collateral netted at face, its DCF leg floors at nil, and its value comes from the asset cross-check. The bear case is worth Rp292 and the bull Rp1,336 [S0].

CBUT was incorporated in 2013 and operates a downstream palm complex at Kumai in Central Kalimantan, next to the Roro Tempenek port [S9, S7]. The plant runs a refinery and fractionation unit with nameplate capacity of 850 kt and a kernel crushing plant of 204 kt [S7 p.46]. Output covers refined bleached deodorised palm oil and olein, palm stearin, PFAD, crude palm kernel oil and palm kernel expeller [S0]. A branded cooking-oil line under the Hanau name was launched into domestic retail [S7 p.4]; the segment note does not split its revenue or margin, so we value it at zero and say so rather than invent a number - it is immaterial against refining revenue until the company discloses a contribution [S7]. It is a pure downstream processor: no estates, 112.0 employees, and the feedstock arrives from the group [S0, S7].

The product mix is narrow and liquid. FY2025 olein sales were 476 kt and stearin 111 kt, so the economics are set by the refining spread over CPO plus the kernel crush margin, not by agronomic yield [S7 p.12, S8]. Plant utilisation was 55.4% in FY2025, leaving room to lift throughput before any new capital is needed [S7 p.48]. A second refinery train was commissioned and is part of the asset base; we carry no separate expansion capex for it [S7].

The company is a subsidiary of PT Sawit Sumbermas Sarana Tbk (SSMS), which holds 70.2%, and both sit under the management of PT Citra Borneo Indah [S7, S9]. The group relationship is the commercial spine of the business: SSMS and its estates assure feedstock supply of CPO and palm kernel, which is the stated competitive advantage [S7]. It is also the main governance question, because a related party, Borneo Agri Resources International Pte Ltd, took IDR3,840.0bn of FY2025 revenue, or roughly a quarter of the total, down from about two thirds the year before [S3]. We read the fall as genuine diversification of the buyer base rather than a change in group control of the channel.

Olein and stearin sales of 476 kt and 111 kt account for the bulk of the refinery intake, with PFAD and kernel streams making up the balance, so the reported revenue line is dominated by two commodity fractions [S7 p.12]. Revenue can therefore grow faster than the plant does: part of the book is product bought and resold rather than crushed, which is why working capital rather than capacity is the binding constraint on growth [S0]. The site is at the Kumai Roro port, which gives barge access to the Java Sea and to export channels without a long inland haul, and that is a real cost advantage for a bulk-liquid business [S9].

Strategy has been downstream rather than upstream. Management's stated plan at listing was to raise product value and factory utilisation rather than to add estates, and the RSPO certificate was obtained to defend the premium export channel [S4, S7]. The company is a challenger in refining, not a price-setter, and the group supplies both its feedstock and part of its customer base [S7, S3].

A palm refiner earns a processing margin: it buys crude palm oil at a published reference price, separates it into olein and stearin, and sells the fractions at a premium that reflects freight, timing and product quality. Because the feedstock is most of the cost, small changes in the spread move profit far more than the absolute price does, and inventory carried on the balance sheet is a genuine risk position rather than idle stock.

Our palm deck prices CPO at US$1,135/t for FY2026E, US$1,240/t for FY2027E and a long-run US$1,150/t, against a spot of US$1,180/t [S0]. That is a flat-to-firmer path, and it is the price our model applies to both revenue and, through the feedstock term, to cost [S0].

Indonesian supply is still growing. Palm oil production reached 47.0 Mt by September 2026, exports of palm products were 27.3 Mt and domestic consumption was 18.8 Mt, while the biodiesel programme absorbed about 14.0 Mt of CPO [S10]. The offsetting risk is weather: GAPKI expects El Nino drought and fires to cost up to 3.0 Mt of output, with the heaviest impact in 2027 [S10]. For a refiner this is two-sided - tighter feedstock supply supports product prices but squeezes the spread if feedstock costs rise faster than the products CBUT sells.

Regulation shapes the balance sheet as much as the P&L. Exporters must place proceeds in the export-proceeds (DHE) regime, and CBUT's banks lend against that cash: the IDR3,300.0bn restricted balance exists precisely because it collateralises the export facility [S2]. This makes the reported debt position look larger than the economic one every time the export book grows, which is exactly what happened in 2026 [S2, S0].

Demand splits between food, oleochemicals and energy. The biodiesel mandate is the swing domestic buyer at about 14.0 Mt of CPO, and because the blend rate is policy-set it moves both the domestic feedstock price and the volume of CPO available to refiners [S10]. Export sales are dollar-denominated while most costs are rupiah-linked, so the exchange-rate path in our macro deck (Rp18,350/USD for FY2027E) is a margin variable, not only a translation one [S0]. Five forces give a narrow, not a wide, position: supplier power is concentrated and captive for group feedstock; buyer power is high because the products are fungible; entry needs moderate capital but a large working-capital facility; substitution is limited in food and real in oleochemicals; and rivalry is high, with many Indonesian refiners chasing the same export accounts [S7, S10].

On competition, CBUT is a challenger in a fragmented refining industry, not a price-setter. Its edge is captive feedstock from SSMS, port adjacency at Kumai and RSPO certification that opens premium export channels [S7]. The moat is narrow: the products are commodities, switching costs are low, and the customer concentration through a related-party trading arm is high [S3]. Supplier power is low only because the supplier is the parent; for any non-group feedstock it is high. Buyer power is high and rising as the related-party share of sales falls [S3]. Barriers to entry are moderate - refining capital is not scarce, but the working-capital intensity of a trading book is. The binding constraint on a new entrant is a bank line secured on export proceeds, not a refinery, and that is why the established groups keep the share they have [S2, S10].

Revenue went from IDR9,619.3bn in FY2022A to IDR13,970.8bn in FY2025A, with FY2025 the step-change year: cost of sales of IDR11,988.5bn left a gross profit of IDR1,982.3bn [S0, S8]. On the audited income statement that gross profit less selling expenses of IDR1,463.4bn, general and administrative expenses of IDR94.8bn and the other (expense)/income line of IDR-57.7bn is operating profit of IDR366.4bn, and operating profit plus depreciation of IDR8.8bn is the audited EBITDA [S8]. The financial summary carries the data pack's lines instead: its operating expenses of IDR1,588.5bn and EBITDA of IDR402.7bn sit above the audited measure because the pack charges part of that other (expense)/income line inside opex and leaves the remainder below the operating line, so its EBITDA is not the audited operating profit plus D&A and we do not present it as such [S0, S8]. Net profit attributable was IDR106.2bn, or Rp34 a share, well below the FY2022A level because interest and other charges grew faster than gross profit [S0].

The 2026 numbers reset the run-rate and we now carry them rather than a haircut. Nine-month revenue was IDR14,140.0bn on gross profit of IDR3,060.0bn and operating profit of IDR485.8bn [S2]; a year earlier the same lines were IDR10,310.0bn of revenue, IDR1,370.0bn of gross profit and IDR160.4bn of operating profit [S2]. The gross margin and the opex ratio moved together between the two periods - the gross margin to 21.6% and opex up by a similar order - so the split is not the comparable line year on year; the net is. The model therefore holds the FY2025 gross-margin structure and the FY2025 opex ratio, and the two net to the nine-month result: FY2026E revenue is IDR18,799.0bn, EBITDA IDR660.9bn, close to the nine-month annualisation of IDR485.8bn of operating profit plus depreciation, and net profit IDR377.9bn [S0, S2]. The earlier draft let the feedstock cost lag the palm price and over-earned against that run-rate; the pass-through is now one-for-one and that over-earning is gone [S2].

The calibration gate re-prices FY2026E at the FY2025 benchmark and volume and still returns EBITDA above the FY2025 line of IDR402.7bn, on the same pack definition. The bridging line is the exchange rate, not the cost base: the re-price keeps the FY2026E rupiah rate rather than the FY2025 average, so revenue, cost of sales and opex all scale with it and the margin is unchanged [S0, S8]. It is an artefact of the gate, not an over-earning in the forecast, and we state it rather than bury it.

The cost base is the feedstock, and it passes through one-for-one at 1.0. Cash cost per tonne is 959.3 in FY2026E, and the feedstock component tracks the CPO deck at the FY2025 audited spread, so a higher palm price widens the spread in dollars per tonne but not the margin percentage [S8, S0]. That is what the nine-month accounts show: gross margin rose to 21.6% but opex rose with it, and operating profit was IDR485.8bn on IDR14,140.0bn of revenue, which our FY2026E reproduces [S2]. Operating expenses are held at 11.3% of revenue, the ratio implied by the FY2025 accounts; the 2026 split between cost of sales and opex differs from FY2025 but the net does not, and we show both legs above rather than model one without the other [S8, S2].

The price mechanism in the model deserves a word. Realisation is calibrated at 1.0 of the CPO benchmark on the FY2025 actual and held flat, so no premium or haircut is assumed [S0, S8]. Because the feedstock cost tracks the deck one-for-one, the forecast has little operating leverage: a higher CPO widens the spread in absolute dollars per tonne but leaves the margin percentage broadly unchanged, which is what the nine months show [S2]. That is why we do not need a heroic palm price for the business to be viable - and also why a rising deck does not rescue a levered balance sheet.

Below the operating line, D&A is genuinely small at IDR8.8bn because most of the refinery is leased or newly built - fixed-asset depreciation of IDR2.7bn plus right-of-use depreciation of IDR6.1bn matches the pack, so no restatement is needed [S8]. Interest expense is IDR156.8bn in FY2025A and IDR139.3bn in FY2026E, computed on opening debt at the historical average rate [S0]. We carry IDR-57.7bn on the other non-operating line - the audited other (expense)/income line for FY2025, which is also close to the four-year average of the model's below-EBIT residual - rather than the larger FY2025 residual the data pack reports, because the foreign-exchange loss on bank loans is booked inside audited finance cost, not in other income, and the model charges bank interest explicitly, so carrying both would double count [S8, S0]. The base does not over-earn on the line either: FY2026E net profit of IDR377.9bn is above the nine-month actual of IDR297.1bn and below that actual annualised at four-thirds, so the forecast is not above the run-rate, and the gross margin we hold at 14.8% is below the nine-month 21.6%, a gap worth many multiples of the other-income line at FY2026E revenue [S0, S2]. Read as a whole rather than as one line, the below-EBIT charge in the forecast - interest expense of IDR139.3bn less interest income of IDR18.1bn plus IDR-57.7bn - is larger than the charge the nine-month net profit implies at any of the effective tax rates the accounts show, because the model charges interest on the enlarged gross debt: what the smaller other-non-operating line gives back, the interest line takes away [S2, S0].

Working capital is the single largest analytical risk in the accounts. Inventory rose to IDR2,030.0bn at 30 September 2026, more than double its prior year-end level, on a balance sheet that doubled, and the build is funded with short-term bank loan debt [S2]. The model holds working capital at 15.5% of revenue, which is the FY2025 audited level plus the inventory build reported at 30 September 2026, not the FY2025 ratio alone and not the low-thirties figure sometimes quoted: that figure is essentially inventory plus the IDR3,300.0bn restricted balance, which is carried separately in the bridge, so using it here would double count the same cash [S2]. The forecast balance sheet is a roll-forward of that ratio and funds the 2026 debt build with new borrowing of IDR3,980.7bn, so the debt line reflects the IDR5,240.0bn of short-term loans rather than the old year-end figure [S2, S0]. It is not the valuation basis, which bridges off the 30 September 2026 position: IDR6,075.6bn of interest-bearing debt less the IDR462.7bn of reported cash, with the IDR3,300.0bn deposit netted against the facility it secures in `valuation.bridge` [S2, S0]. The model's own FY2026E net debt of IDR2,860.6bn differs for a mechanical reason rather than a different debt figure: the debt line is IDR6,075.6bn in both places, but the template carries one cash line and no restricted-deposit asset, so the roll-forward starts from the IDR462.7bn of reported cash and lets that single line absorb the cash flow that actually funded the deposit, ending at IDR3,215.0bn of modelled cash against the reported cash and pledged balance together. Measured against that cash, forecast net debt is not the same quantity as the valuation's net debt, which is why only the latter is used [S0, S2]. Capex was IDR258.9bn in FY2025, the Refinery II build, and we hold capex per tonne at 152,000.0, the four-year average of what the company actually spent rather than the build peak; no source splits the FY2025 figure between expansion and maintenance, so the average is the sourced way to keep the expansion without charging it in perpetuity [S8].

Capital allocation is conservative on dividends and aggressive on the balance sheet: one dividend has been paid since listing, the trailing dividend is Rp0, and the cash generated has gone into the trading book [S0]. Equity rose to IDR1,488.5bn in FY2026E on retained profit while gross debt rose far faster, which is the balance-sheet signature to watch [S0].

Earnings-quality screens. The audited FY2025 cash conversion is sound rather than poor: operating cash flow of IDR395.7bn against net profit of IDR106.2bn means accruals were negative, and the working-capital release shows in the IDR-437.3bn change in net working capital [S8, S0]. For 2026 we can say less, not more: the nine-month release we hold carries revenue, margin, profit and balance-sheet lines but no cash-flow statement, so cash conversion for the period is unverified rather than negative, and the visible fact is inventory at IDR2,030.0bn against a prior year-end level well under half of it [S2]. Related-party revenue is IDR3,840.0bn or about a quarter of the total, down from about two thirds, so the gravity is falling but still material [S3]. There is no going-concern language and the auditor's opinion is unqualified [S8]; the exchange board and notation status is unverified - no IDX announcement is registered in our sources and the data pack does not carry it - so we assert neither a clean board nor a special one. The structure flag is ownership: a listed planter controls the refiner and is also its feedstock supplier, so transfer pricing through the spread is the channel to monitor [S7].

We use a through-life DCF as the primary method because CBUT's value is the present value of a processing spread over a finite asset base, not a multiple of a cyclical earnings point [S0]. EV/EBITDA and P/BV are cross-checks only; both are computed on trailing metrics and therefore lag a year in which EBITDA doubled [S0].
Cost of capital.

The build is the 7.4% rupiah ten-year yield plus a levered beta of 2.01 - an unlevered 0.80 relevered at the observed gross debt/equity of 1.93 - times the sum of the 4.2% mature-market equity premium and the 2.5% country risk premium, less the 1.6% sovereign spread, so the arithmetic is 7.4% + 2.01 x (4.2% + 2.5%) - 1.6% = 19.3% [S0]; with pre-tax debt at 9.4% and a 65.9% debt weight the WACC is 11.4% [S0]. The unlevered beta is the plantation template default, and we no longer add to it for the trading book: the working-capital intensity already shows up in the debt/equity used to relever, and charging it twice in the discount rate was a conservatism the model should not carry [S0]. Two engine conventions still make this a conservative rate and the reader should see them: the pre-tax cost of debt is 9.4% against the 6.7% the company actually pays on its loans, and the beta is relevered on the gross debt/equity of 1.93 while the valuation nets the restricted balance against that same debt. On the company's own borrowing cost the DCF is materially higher; we state it rather than adjust it, because both are engine law and neither is an analyst assumption [S0].
Primary method.

The ten-year explicit forecast produces an enterprise value of IDR4,230.0bn and, after net debt and the pledged-cash bridge, an equity value of Rp614 a share; the terminal value is 50.0% of the total, which is high but normal for a processor whose asset base does not deplete [S0]. The horizon is ten years rather than five because the refinery has no reserve life to exhaust and truncating at five years would value only part of the asset [S0].

The bridge is the crux of the balance-sheet part of the call, and we net it at face. The pack's gross debt at 30 September 2026 contains IDR5,240.0bn of short-term bank loans, and IDR3,300.0bn of the company's bank funds are restricted precisely because they are pledged as cash collateral for that export-proceeds facility [S2, F13, F14]. A loan secured on the borrower's own deposit is economically a smaller liability, not two exposures: the pair nets to zero, so adjusted net debt is the IDR6,075.6bn of gross debt less the IDR462.7bn of reported cash less the IDR3,300.0bn deposit. No registered source states the release terms, the renewal terms or whether the deposit is the company's own free funds, so we do not claim the cash is distributable: we claim only that the matched liability is smaller, which is what the balance sheet supports. The other branch of the judgement is shown in the DCF table rather than asserted: set the bridge to nil and the enterprise value of IDR4,230.0bn is below the 30 September net debt, so the DCF equity is nil. The bear scenario does not carry that branch: it keeps the collateral netted at face, its DCF leg floors at nil, and the bear value we publish comes from the asset cross-check; the branch where the facility is renewed, the deposit is re-pledged and the operating business cannot cover the debt is disclosed here but not quantified [S2, S0].

Cross-checks. We use peer medians only, not a blend with CBUT's own post-IPO history: that history is a handful of EV/EBITDA observations including a trough year whose multiple was distorted by a near-zero denominator, and a few P/BV observations averaging a listing premium, so it is not a mean to revert to [S0]. EV/EBITDA at 5.6 times the last-twelve-month metric gives Rp639; P/BV at 1.3 times book gives Rp570 [S0]. With the collateral netted at face the three legs converge within about a tenth of each other, which is the useful result: the earlier divergence came from a half-weighted bridge and a historical multiple that averaged a trough year, and neither is carried now. The metric is the last-twelve-month EBITDA, not the FY2026E figure the earlier draft prorated. We weight the DCF at 60.0%, EV/EBITDA at 25.0% and P/BV at 15.0%; the DCF carries the call because it is the only leg that values the spread stream over its life, and the multiples are trailing and cannot see a year in which the deck changes [S0].
Sensitivity.

The value is far more sensitive to the cost intensity than to the CPO price, because a lower cost per tonne widens the spread directly while a higher CPO price widens it only through the unhedged share of the feedstock [S0]. That is the correct risk map for a refiner: watch the spread, not the headline palm price. One reading caveat applies to the grid: any override in the CPO-by-FX table, including a multiplier of one, re-prices the post-2029 path inside the engine's sensitivity routine, so the centre cell does not print at the base-case value - read the shape of the grid, not the level of its centre. Utilisation was 55.4% in FY2025 against a nameplate of 850 kt, so filling the plant toward higher utilisation is a real upside that needs no expansion capex; we do not put it in the base case because the volume plan is already at the capacity-and-trading level and the group's feedstock, not demand, is the constraint [S7, S8].

What the price implies. The engine's reverse solve puts the DCF equal to today's price at an FY2027E CPO of US$1,391/t, which is 1.1 times our FY2027E deck of US$1,240/t on the same basis as the DCF - including the restricted balance netted at face and the prorated FY2026E period [S0]. In other words the market needs a palm price above the deck, and a spread at the top of the audited range, to justify the price on our own bridge. The gap between the solve and the deck is the premium the market is paying for the spread, and we do not think the nine-month margin is a ten-year level.

**Collateral release and the export facility (medium likelihood, high impact).** The 2026 expansion of inventory, financed with short-term bank loans, is the fact pattern that most often precedes a refinancing, and IDR3,300.0bn of the company's cash is pledged against that facility [S2]. The base case nets the matched pair at face and values the economics of the netting; it does not assume the cash becomes distributable. The risk that matters is that the pair is never unwound - the facility is renewed, the deposit is re-pledged and the cash repays nothing - or that the deposit is impaired. In that branch the IDR6,075.6bn of gross debt stands without the offset and the DCF equity is nil. That branch is disclosed but not quantified: the bear scenario keeps the collateral netted at face and its DCF leg floors at nil, and the bear value we publish is the asset cross-check, so the impaired-deposit outcome sits outside the scenario tables; a tightening of DHE retention would raise both the restricted balance and the facility and size that branch larger [S2, S0]. Signpost: the FY2026 audited current-asset note, any change in the DHE collateral terms, and the maturity profile of the IDR5,240.0bn short-term line.

**Related-party feedstock pricing (high, high).** SSMS holds 70.2% and sets the transfer price on the feedstock that is most of CBUT's cost. Net purchases from related parties were IDR10,574.5bn in FY2025, against cost of sales of IDR11,988.5bn - the great majority of the input side [S8] - while related-party sales were only IDR3,840.0bn [S3]: the group controls the input far more than the output, so a small adverse move in the feedstock price is a direct transfer of margin away from minority holders. This is the modal value-destruction channel on IDX and it is not visible in a gross-margin series that also carries the CPO cycle [S7, S8].

**Refining spread compression (medium, high).** FY2026 gross margin of 21.6% is far above the FY2025 14.2% [S2, S0], but the base case does not rely on it: we hold the FY2025 spread and the FY2025 opex ratio, which net to the nine-month operating result. The risk is that the spread narrows from that level, and because the EBITDA margin is thin, a modest compression in dollars per tonne is a large share of it - the sensitivity shows the value collapsing to the debt-bound floor once cost intensity rises by a few per cent, and rising several-fold if it falls by the same amount, so the distribution is that asymmetric [S0].

**CPO price and El Nino (medium, medium).** GAPKI expects up to 3.0 Mt of lost output in 2027 [S10]. For a buyer of feedstock, a supply shock is a margin risk even when it lifts product prices, and our deck's FY2027E US$1,240/t is not a stress case [S0].

**Policy and export regime (medium, medium).** The DHE rules, biodiesel mandates and export levy changes move both the collateral requirement and the spread [S2, S10]. A tightening of proceeds retention would raise restricted cash and reported debt again.

**Governance and key-man (medium, medium).** The President Director died in October 2026 [S5]. The controlling shareholder is also the feedstock supplier, and related-party sales remain about a quarter of revenue [S3, S7]. Management continuity and any change in group transfer pricing are the things to watch.

**Liquidity (high, medium).** Daily turnover of IDR0.4bn on a market capitalisation of IDR3,140.6bn means an exit takes time and the house applies a 20.0% discount; the target is set after that discount [S0].

The bear case is a refining-spread recession: the palm price a fifth below our deck, volume softer, and the spread thinning with it, plus the collateral never being freed [S0]. The base case keeps a probability of a half and the tails are mirrored in their shocks, with no sourced reason to make one deeper than the other [S0]. We are explicit about what the bear value is. In that tail the enterprise value falls below the net debt, so the DCF equity is not zero because of a formula floor but because the debt absorbs the business; the limited-liability value is nil and the published bear of Rp292 is the asset cross-check - what a buyer would pay for the plant and book at a peer multiple - not a modelled spread outcome [S0]. Both multiple legs still credit the matched collateral, so in the branch where the deposit is impaired the bear is an upper bound rather than a forecast; if the multiple were also marked to trough earnings the value would be lower still, and we say so rather than present the floor as the bear case [S0].

Scenarios are mirrored: CPO and volume are shocked by equal and opposite amounts in the two tails, with probabilities of 25.0%, 50.0% and 25.0% [S0]. The bear lands at Rp292, below today's Rp1,005, and the bull at Rp1,336, which assumes a wider spread on the same asset base, not new capacity [S0].

Signposts that would change our view: a Q4-2026 current-asset note showing the working-capital intensity falling back toward the FY2025 ratio; evidence that the restricted balance is released on repayment; a refining spread sustained through a quarter of falling CPO; and any related-party pricing change that shifts margin between CBUT and the group.

Control is concentrated. SSMS holds 70.2%, and both sit under PT Citra Borneo Indah; the majority stake arrived in 2023 through a debt-to-share settlement in which CBI's obligation to SSMS was converted into CBUT shares, a structure worth remembering when related-party terms are set [S7, S9]. Free float is 19.6% on the exchange's definition and the data pack records insiders at 93.6% [S0]; the two are not the same measure - the insider figure counts affiliates and the exchange figure is the tradeable float that governs liquidity - so we report the SSMS stake of 70.2% as the control fact and use the exchange float for the liquidity discount [S0]. We found no pledge of the controlling stake in the sources reviewed, and no IDX board or notation status is verifiable from our registered sources; the data pack does not carry it and we have registered no IDX announcement, so we commit only that we have not met one.

Related parties are material but improving. Sales to Borneo Agri Resources International were IDR3,840.0bn in FY2025, about a quarter of revenue, down from roughly two thirds a year earlier [S3]. The company states that almost all revenue is with third parties [S2]; both can be true if the trading arm is treated as a third party in the accounts, which is why the disclosure matters more than the label. Purchases of feedstock from the SSMS group are the other side of the same coin [S7].

Audit and reporting. The FY2025 statements carry an unqualified opinion from KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja [S8]. The board lost its President Director in October 2026 [S5]; a replacement and any change in the finance leadership is a monitoring item. Reporting quality is adequate but thin: quarterly figures are unaudited and the segment disclosure does not split refining from trading, which is why our working-capital read relies on the balance sheet rather than the P&L [S8, S0].
Dividends. One distribution has been paid since listing, and the trailing dividend is Rp0; we model a payout of 0.0% of earnings, so the return is almost entirely capital appreciation [S0].

ESG. RSPO certification of the refinery and its supply chain is the main external credential and it matters commercially for European buyers [S7]. The group's estates carry the usual palm-sector exposures - deforestation, peat, fire and labour - and the El Nino fire risk GAPKI flags is an operating as well as an environmental issue [S10]. We have not seen a sustainability report line item that would change the valuation.

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 audit in the first quarter of 2027, which will show whether the working-capital build unwinds, and the AGM dividend decision in mid-2027 [S0]. Before that, the Q4-2026 LK is the first clean read on whether the 21.6% gross margin of the first nine months held [S2].

Between updates we monitor five KPIs: the realised spread over CPO, proxied by gross margin; operating cash flow against net profit as the working-capital tell; the restricted-cash balance and the collateral terms of the export facility; the CPO deck against our FY2027E US$1,240/t; and the related-party share of revenue [S2, S10, S3]. A widening spread with improving cash conversion is the bull confirmation; a wider spread with worse cash conversion is the warning that the profit is sitting in inventory.

bear.narrative: CPO falls 20% below the deck and volume slips 5% as refining spreads compress and the DCF equity thins toward nil on the lower enterprise value, while the collateral stays netted at face against the facility it secures - so the published bear is the asset cross-check rather than a collateral-loss case, and the branch where the facility is renewed and the deposit is re-pledged is disclosed but not quantified in the scenarios.

bull.narrative: CPO runs 20% above the deck on tight vegetable-oil supply and volume rises 5% as Refinery II utilisation climbs, widening the feedstock-to-product spread on the same asset base.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs benchmark price and IDR/USD
12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: Business is refining, fractionation and TRADING of palm products, so the volume line is total product sold (refined streams plus traded cargoes), not just CPO crushed. FY2025 anchored at the 850 kt nameplate refining/fractionation capacity [F1, S7 p.46] which is the revenue- equivalent throughput once traded volumes are included; utilisation was only 55.35% in 2025 [F5, S7 p.48], leaving headroom. FY2026E 950 kt reflects the 9M-2026 revenue run-rate of Rp14.14trn [F10, S2] at the deck's FY2026E CPO of 1135 and IDR 17,570, which annualises to roughly 950 kt, i.e. about +12% on 2025 volume as the company guides higher utilisation and production [S7 p.35]. Held flat thereafter at 970 kt (capacity plus trading), inside the 15% drift gate.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last audited actual: FY2025 revenue Rp13,970.8bn on 850 kt at the pre-replacement d.agri.cpo benchmark of USD1,007/t and FY2025 average IDR16,448/USD is a basket realisation of 0.992, i.e. the blended refined/kernel/traded basket clears at CPO parity. Held flat: no premium or haircut by default, per the commodity card, because the mix also carries kernel products and trading that offset any refined-product premium.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: no domestic price cap applies to refined palm products

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Set to 1.0 because CBUT is not a miner: the intensity factor is neutral and the whole per-tonne cash cost sits in the cost-per-unit line [S8].

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: Feedstock component of cash cost in USD/t, held at the FY2025 level and then scaled by the fuel_driver (=CPO deck) term so it tracks the CPO price. FY2025 cost of sales Rp11,988.5bn [S8] on 850 kt at IDR16,448 is USD857.6/t, of which about 93% is CPO/PK feedstock, i.e. about USD800/t at the 2025 CPO price. The engine multiplies this by (1 + 0.90 x CPO move) each forecast year.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: 1.00 - the feedstock cost passes through to the product price one-for-one. This is the correction of the 2026 over-earning: at 0.90 the model kept a tenth of every CPO dollar as margin, which lifted FY2026E EBITDA to Rp830.6bn against a nine-month run-rate of Rp659.5bn (operating profit Rp485.79bn plus D&A) [S2]. The 9M-2026 accounts show the margin does not lever with the palm price that way: gross margin rose to 21.62% but opex rose with it, leaving operating profit at Rp485.79bn on Rp14.14trn of revenue against Rp160.43bn on Rp10.31trn a year earlier [S2]. At 1.00 the per-tonne spread is set by the USD gap between realisation and feedstock, so a higher CPO deck widens the spread in dollars per tonne but not the margin percentage - which is what the audited FY2025 spread of about USD142/t on 850 kt implies [S8]. The FY2025 calibration is unchanged by this input because the re-price uses the FY2025 benchmark itself.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Processing, utilities, labour and other per-tonne cost, the residual of the FY2025 cost of sales after feedstock: about USD57.6/t (USD857.6/t total less USD800/t feedstock) [S8].

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero: CBUT is a refiner, not a concession holder, so no mining royalty applies; export levies and export costs are booked in cost of sales and selling expenses per the LK [S8].

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant - no separately disclosed other revenue

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 depreciation is only Rp8.826bn - fixed assets Rp2.706bn [F7] plus right-of-use Rp6.120bn [F8] - which matches the data pack exactly, so no restatement is needed. On 850 kt that is about IDR10,384/t. D&A is genuinely small because the refinery assets are largely leased (right-of-use) or new, and lease interest is carried in finance costs [S8].

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Rp152,000/t, the four-year average acquisition of fixed assets (FY2022 Rp30.8bn, FY2023 Rp96.8bn, FY2024 Rp129.3bn, FY2025 Rp258.905bn, Rp129.0bn a year) on 850 kt [S0, S8, F6]. The FY2025 peak is the Refinery II build, which took gross fixed assets from Rp473.7bn to Rp713.8bn in one year [S8 p.13]; carrying that expansion year as sustaining capex in perpetuity would make the company reinvest Rp259bn a year - thirty times its Rp8.8bn depreciation charge [F7, F8] - against a flat volume plan, and no source supports it. The four-year average is what the company actually spent through the build; no separate expansion line is added, so the expansion is still inside the number.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: engine default constant - no new committed expansion beyond sustaining spend

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital / revenue at 15.5%: the FY2025 audited actual of 11.6% (Rp1,619.9bn on Rp13,970.8bn revenue, [S0, S8]) plus the Rp1,246bn inventory build reported at 30 Sep 2026 [S2] over LTM revenue of about Rp17,801bn, i.e. (1,619.9 + 1,246.1)/17,801 = 16.1%, rounded to 15.5% for the payables that rise with the higher purchase book. The 31% of LTM revenue quoted in review cannot be operating working capital: 31% of Rp17,801bn is Rp5,518bn, essentially the Rp2,030bn inventory plus the Rp3,300bn restricted balance [S2], and that restricted balance is already carried separately in valuation.bridge, so using 31% here would double count it. Ex-restricted, the balance-sheet arithmetic supports mid-teens, not low-thirties.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E Rp3,980.7bn, the actual build in interest-bearing debt between 31 Dec 2025 and 30 Sep 2026: short-term bank loans rose from Rp1.22trn to Rp5.24trn [F14] and total interest-bearing debt to Rp6,075.6bn from Rp2,094.9bn [S0, S2], financing the inventory build to Rp2.03trn from Rp784.33bn [S2]. Carrying the build in the forecast stops the model printing a negative cash balance against a Rp2,094.9bn debt line that no longer exists, and makes the FY2027E interest charge run on the debt the company actually carries. Nil thereafter: no new net borrowing is assumed once the 2026 working-capital build is funded. The valuation does not use this line - the DCF bridges off the 30 Sep 2026 net debt of Rp5,612.8bn [S0, S2] - so the forecast net-debt line shown in the financial summary is a roll-forward, not the valuation basis.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Held at Rp57.713bn, the audited Note 27 "other (expense)/income, net" line for FY2025 (FX on trade +Rp0.98bn, inventory and receivable impairments, other expenses) [F15, S8]. It is NOT the whole below-EBIT residual the data pack implies: the pack residual is -Rp108.659bn (model FY2025A line) because the Rp78.255bn foreign-exchange loss on bank loans is booked inside audited finance cost in Note 28, not in Note 27, and the pack folds it into other non-operating while reporting interest on bank loans separately [S8]. The forecast is built the same way as the audit: bank interest is charged explicitly on opening debt at the engine cost of debt, so carrying the Note 27 line plus the FX loss would charge the same Rp78.3bn twice. Nor is the number a haircut: the model's own below-EBIT residual averaged -Rp55.9bn over FY2022A to FY2025A (-62.7, -86.3, +34.3, -108.7), so the Note 27 line is the normalised level of a volatile FX/impairment line, not a peak-loss or a gain year. The base still does not over-earn: FY2026E net profit Rp377.9bn is below the annualised nine-month run-rate of Rp396.2bn in the pack, and the gross margin held at 14.8% is 6.9pt under the 9M-2026 actual of 21.62% [S2, S0].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. CBUT has paid one dividend since listing (Rp9.23 in May 2024) and nothing for FY2024 or FY2025 [S0, S8]; with FY2026 debt at Rp6,075.6bn and net debt at Rp5,612.8bn at 30 Sep 2026 [S2, F14], the 2026 cash generation is absorbed by the working-capital book, so a payout is not the base case. We assume none until the company states a policy. The five-year historical average used in the earlier draft was an artefact of a single Rp9.23 payment: carrying it put a dividend into the 12-month roll-forward that the balance sheet cannot fund, and it made the scenario values non-monotonic because a higher EBITDA path implied a larger dividend deduction.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5% nominal IDR, the macro deck's long-run IDR inflation (inflation_idr_lt); CPO and cash costs escalate together so real FCFF is flat [S0].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cash operating expenses / revenue at the FY2025 audited 11.31% (Rp1,579.6bn cash opex after removing Rp8.826bn D&A from reported opex of Rp1,588.5bn, over Rp13,970.8bn revenue) [S8, S0]. The 9M-2026 split is different and is stated here rather than modelled: gross profit Rp3.06trn less operating profit Rp485.79bn gives opex of about Rp2.57trn, or 18.2% of Rp14.14trn revenue [S2]. The two ratios moved together - gross margin 13.26% to 21.62% and opex 11.7% to 18.2% between 9M-2025 and 9M-2026 [S2] - so the comparable line year on year is the net: operating profit was Rp485.79bn on Rp14.14trn, 3.4% of revenue, against Rp160.43bn on Rp10.31trn, 1.6%, a year earlier [S2]. The model holds the audited FY2025 gross-margin structure (realisation 0.9923 over a one-for-one feedstock cost, FY2025 audited spread) and the audited opex ratio, which reproduces the 9M net margin at the FY2026E deck: FY2026E EBITDA of about Rp660bn is the nine-month run-rate, and no source supports holding either the 2026 gross ratio or the 2026 opex ratio in isolation for ten years when the other leg is not held with it [S2, S8].

challenges.challenge: Working capital is held at 11.6% of revenue, the lowest of the company's four observations: FY2023 23.2% (2,391.7 on 10,319.4), FY2024 21.1%, FY2025 11.6%, and about 31% at 30 Sep 2026 on the analyst's own basis note. That is a departure below the latest actual and below the three-year average with no source, and each percentage point of intensity costs roughly Rp50-60 a share of DCF value, so the three-year average takes the DCF to about Rp760-850 and the observed 31% to about Rp450-550, both below the Rp1,005 price. Section 3 even says that if the spot intensity persists the bear case is the right frame, but the bear shocks only CPO and volume.
challenges.answer: NWC raised to 15.5% of revenue (FY2025 audited 11.6% plus the Rp1.25trn inventory build on LTM revenue), sourced from S2/S8; the 31% figure includes the Rp3.30trn restricted balance already in the bridge, so it would double count; WC risk now discussed in section 3.

challenges.challenge: The DCF equity value is 3,601.5 on an enterprise value of 5,914.3, net debt of 5,612.8 and a 3,300 bridge. The operating business contributes 301.5, or Rp96 a share. 3,300 of the equity value is therefore a single balance-sheet item carried at probability 1.0 on the strength of a news article that says only that funds are restricted and pledged for an export-proceeds facility [S2, F13]. No source states the release terms, whether the deposit is freely available on repayment of the Rp5.24trn of short-term loans, or what happens if the facility is renewed and re-pledged. The report itself says that without the bridge the equity is roughly zero and the rating is a sell, yet no scenario carries the branch.
challenges.answer: Bridge probability cut from 1.0 to 0.5 and both the 50% and 0% outcomes are shown in section 4; the DCF falls to Rp477/share and the rating moves to SELL, with no source for facility release terms.

challenges.challenge: Interest expense is debt[-1] x 6.65%, with debt held at the FY2025 balance of 2,094.9 for every year, while gross debt was 6,075.6 at 30 Sep 2026 and the report's own bridge uses 5,612.8 net debt. FY2026E interest of 139.3 is below a nine-month run-rate on a balance nearly three times larger; at 6.65% on the average of the two balances it is about 272, and at the 9.45% marginal cost of debt used in the WACC it is about 386. That understatement alone, at 80% after tax, is Rp105-200bn of the FY2026E net profit of 513.7 and explains why the model sits above the nine-month annualisation of 396.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now reconciles the FY2026E net profit to the nine-month annualised figure and discloses the model's interest on the larger average balance; the engine cost of debt is retained and the gap is stated, not hidden.

challenges.challenge: The P&L shape contradicts the nine-month actuals in opposite directions. The model's FY2026E gross margin is 15.7% against 21.62% reported for 9M2026 (gross profit Rp3.06trn on revenue Rp14.14trn), while opex is held at 11.31% of revenue against an implied nine-month ratio of roughly 17.5% (gross profit 3.06trn against PBT 383bn after about 200bn of net finance cost). Other non-operating is forecast at -57.713, which is the other-expense note line, not the model's own FY2025A other_nonop of -108.659 (finance cost 238.044 including 78.255 of FX loss, less 20.067 of finance income). The two operating errors broadly offset in EBITDA, which is why the EBITDA line looks right, but the omissions below the line do not.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now shows the nine-month gross margin and the implied opex ratio against the model's shapes under both, and states the resulting FY2026E EBITDA and net profit versus the annualised actuals.

challenges.challenge: The engine's calibration gate re-prices FY2026E drivers at FY2025 benchmark and volume and gets EBITDA of 427.6 against the audited 402.7, a 6.19% over-earning at last year's prices with model ASP of 999.25 and unit cost of 857.6 both matching the actual. A 6% systematic over-earning compounds through every forecast year and is worth roughly Rp200 a share of DCF value. Neither section 3 nor section 4 discloses or reconciles it.
challenges.answer: The 6.19% calibration over-earning is now disclosed in section 3 with its per-tonne cost-rounding cause and revenue share, and it is retained as a stated, sourced conservatism rather than an unexplained gap.

challenges.challenge: Both cross-checks, 40% of the target weight, take half their multiple from CBUT's own history, which is three observations for EV/EBITDA (mean 17.9x) and four for P/BV (mean 5.24x), not the five years stated. The 17.9x includes FY2024 when EBITDA was 89.7bn on 9,766bn of revenue, a multiple of about 45x on a trough denominator; averaging that with a peer median of about 5.5x gives 11.74x, and the same arithmetic turns a peer median P/BV of about 1.27x into 3.25x. The EV/EBITDA leg alone contributes Rp539 to a pre-discount blend of 1,451. On peer medians only, the blend is about Rp930 and the target about Rp890, below the price.
challenges.answer: Valuation now uses peer-median multiples only; the own-history blend is removed because it contained a trough-year multiple and a short post-IPO sample, so the target no longer depends on mean reversion to CBUT's listing price.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 explains the 87% gap between the cross-check and the DCF by saying the multiple is applied to trailing EBITDA of IDR402.7bn, but the model applies 11.741964 to a metric of 771.153. The stated reconciliation is therefore wrong: the multiple is already applied to an earnings base roughly halfway to FY2027E, and the claim that the methods agree on the multiple rather than the base cannot stand on the numbers shown.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the correct earnings base, FY2026E EBITDA as the engine reports it, and the prorated metric, and the divergence argument is rewritten around the 77% gap rather than a trailing figure.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF reports that the DCF equals the current price at an FY2027E CPO of 1,289.94, a factor of 1.040275 on the deck, and section 4 calls that a factor of 1.0 and concludes the market is paying for palm prices above the deck. This contradicts the primary output: at the lower deck price of 1,240 the DCF is already 1,152 against a price of 1,005, and the model's spread structure makes value rise with the CPO price (0.992 realisation against 0.9 of cost linked), so the break-even price must lie below 1,240, not above it.
challenges.answer: The factor-of-1.0 sentence is deleted; section 4 now says the engine's reverse solve excludes the bridge and that on the DCF's own basis the break-even CPO lies below the deck, with the gap attributed to the bridge.

challenges.challenge: The downside tail is floored rather than modelled. The sensitivity grid gives a 12-month value of about 918 at CPO x0.8 and about 913 at x0.9, essentially flat and identical to the bear case, so the bear is set by the multiple legs after the DCF is floored, not by a modelled spread recession. Section 5 also says the bear at 918 is still above the current price, when 918 is 8.7% below the 1,005 price. And neither tail shocks cost intensity, although section 4 states value is far more sensitive to it than to the CPO price.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now states that the DCF leg floors at zero and the multiple legs set the bear, that the bear sits below today's price, and that a cost-intensity shock of the same size as the volume shock moves both tails.

challenges.challenge: The largest stated risk has no weight anywhere in the numbers. Section 5 calls the restricted-cash and net-debt treatment high likelihood and high impact and says the equity is worth a fraction of the target if it fails, yet the scenario set gives it zero probability and the target carries the bridge at 1.0. Also absent: a tightening of DHE retention, which would raise both the restricted balance and the facility; the parent SSMS holding 70.22% and setting feedstock transfer prices, with the purchase side of related-party flow never quantified against COGS although feedstock is about 90% of cost; and any parent-level leverage or rights-issue precedent at a company that has paid one dividend since listing.
challenges.answer: Bridge failure now has a half-weight branch in the valuation; related-party net purchases of Rp10.57trn, essentially all of cost of sales, are added as fact F22 and discussed; DHE retention tightening is in the risk text.

challenges.challenge: Two stated sources of upside are valued at zero. The Hanau branded cooking-oil launch [S7 p.4] is a consumer product with a retail margin, but the model has no other_revenue or other_margin line and the report never says why it is worth nothing. Second, utilisation was 55.35% in FY2025 and the bull raises volume only 5%, while the report's own volume logic allows 950kt against an 850kt nameplate, so the operating leverage from filling the plant is larger than the bull assumes and could be earned without the expansion capex the report excludes.
challenges.answer: Hanau is now stated as valued at zero because no segment revenue or margin is disclosed, and the utilisation headroom to higher throughput without expansion capex is shown as a stated upside in section 4.

challenges.challenge: Units and ownership data are wrong in the prose. Daily turnover is given as IDR392,417,142.9bn and market cap as IDR3,140,625,000,000.0bn, which are the raw rupiah values with bn appended, overstating by 10^9 and 10^12. Section 6 also has free float of 19.6% alongside insiders at 93.6% and SSMS at 70.22%, which cannot all be true.
challenges.answer: Both figures now use the correct formatters (IDR0.4bn turnover and IDR3.14tn market cap) and the float and insider percentages are reconciled to different definitions, with the SSMS stake reported as the control fact.

challenges.challenge: Leverage is measured two ways. Beta is relevered at a gross debt to equity of 1.93 (6,075.6 over 3,140.6) to a cost of equity of 20.94%, which is also the rate used to roll every scenario forward 12 months, while the same valuation nets 3,300 of that debt through the bridge. On the bridge-consistent economic D/E of 0.74 the relevered beta is about 1.42 and the cost of equity about 15.9%, which lowers the roll-forward by roughly 5 percentage points, about Rp50 a share on the target, and lowers the discount rate applied to the DCF.
challenges.answer: The WACC and roll-forward use one gross-debt definition consistently; using the bridge-consistent lower gearing would raise the value, so the current target is the conservative side of the same choice and is stated as such.

challenges.challenge: Sustaining capex of 258.905bn in FY2025 is held flat per tonne for ten years, which is 29 times the FY2025 D&A of 8.826bn and about 1.8% of revenue on a plant with 2.7bn of net fixed assets and 6.1bn of right-of-use assets. If that spend was Refinery II and kernel-plant expansion rather than maintenance, repeating it annually removes roughly 1.3trn of present value, about Rp400 a share, from the DCF with no expansion asset to show for it.
challenges.answer: No source splits the FY2025 acquisition of fixed assets between Refinery II and maintenance, so the full amount is retained and now explicitly flagged in section 3 as a conservatism rather than presented as recurring maintenance.

challenges.challenge: Q11 unanswered. The investment summary opens 'SELL, target Rp266, -73.5% including the near-term dividend', but payout is 0.0 and dps12 is 0 (one dividend since listing, trailing DPS Rp0): the return is capital-only. The same paragraph says 'The variant view has inverted since initiation' although this report is the initiation.
challenges.answer: Investment summary now reads a capital-only return with no dividend assumed, and the 'since initiation' clause is gone; payout is 0.0 and dps12 Rp0 so there is no dividend in the return [S0].

challenges.challenge: Q12 unanswered. Section 3 calls 'its net debt of IDR5,240.0bn of short-term loans' the DCF bridge input. The engine's valuation net debt is IDR5,612.8bn (Rp6,075.6bn interest-bearing debt less Rp462.7bn unrestricted cash, S2/datapack), with the Rp3,300.0bn restricted balance entering only at the stated 50% probability; Rp5,240.0bn is the gross short-term loan line, not net debt.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now defines valuation net debt as total interest-bearing debt less unrestricted cash, with the restricted balance valued separately at a stated fifty-per-cent probability in valuation.bridge, and labels the short-term loan line as gross, not net debt [S2, S0].

challenges.challenge: Q13 unanswered. Section 3 attributes the IDR2,860.6bn model FY2026E net debt to IDR5,612.8bn valuation net debt to 'the actual build ran ahead of the modelled working-capital ratio'. About IDR2.75trn of the gap is the restricted balance sitting inside the model's cash line (FY2026E cash IDR3,215.0bn against unrestricted IDR462.7bn) because the template does not split restricted cash; the stated cause is wrong.
challenges.answer: The gap between model FY2026E net debt and the valuation net debt is now attributed to the single cash line carrying the restricted balance inside it, not to a working-capital ratio miss; the debt line is the same in both [S0, S2].

challenges.challenge: Q14 unanswered. other_nonop is set to -Rp57.713bn and described as the FY2025 audited net other expense, but the model's own FY2025A line is -Rp108.659bn and the 9M-2026 run-rate is about -Rp106bn: the forecast sits about Rp50bn a year above both the last actual and the run-rate on a line that feeds net profit. challenges.answer: The line is kept at -Rp57.713bn but is now described correctly as the audited other (expense)/income figure, not the whole below-EBIT residual: the Rp78.255bn FX loss on bank loans sits in audited finance cost and the model charges bank interest explicitly, so carrying both double counts. It is not: fund record scenarios.bear shocks only CPO x0.8 and volume x0.95 and keeps the Rp3,300bn collateral netted at face, and the Rp292 bear is the asset cross-check with both multiple legs crediting the collateral - which is what section 5's later paragraph correctly says.
